title: Teeba Obaid
text: Hello! I’m Teeba Obaid. I am a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia. Before MDS, I completed a PhD in Educational Psychology and developed experience in research, instructional design, and data analysis through my academic work. I am especially interested in machine learning and hope to continue building my skills for data science and machine learning roles.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
In this post, I explore the penguins dataset using R. I use the data and plotting techniques from my DSCI 523 R Programming lab to compare penguin measurements across species.
I focus on the relationship between bill length and body mass. I also explore how the order of species categories affects the presentation of a plot.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
In this post, I explore the penguins dataset using R. I use the data and plotting techniques from my DSCI 523 R Programming lab to compare penguin measurements across species.
I focus on the relationship between bill length and body mass. I also explore how the order of species categories affects the presentation of a plot.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
Data Source
I use the penguins dataset from the palmerpenguins R package. I worked with this dataset in DSCI 523 R Programming.
The dataset contains measurements of Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
Loading the Data
First, I load the packages and display the first six rows of the dataset.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
Comparing Penguin Species
I first compare the average bill length and body mass of the three penguin species. I remove missing values so they do not affect the calculations.

penguin_summary <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(
    mean_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

penguin_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_bill_length mean_body_mass
  <fct>                <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Adelie                38.8          3701.
2 Chinstrap             48.8          3733.
3 Gentoo                47.5          5076.



What the Summary Shows
Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass, while Chinstrap penguins have the longest average bill length. Adelie penguins have the shortest average bill length of the three species.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
Bill Length and Body Mass
I use a scatter plot to compare bill length and body mass. Each colour represents a different penguin species.

penguins_original <- ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  xlab("Bill length (mm)") +
  ylab("Body mass (g)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18))

penguins_original

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).










What the Scatter Plot Shows
The scatter plot shows a positive relationship between bill length and body mass within the penguin species. Gentoo penguins generally have a higher body mass than the other two species. Adelie penguins tend to have shorter bills, while Chinstrap penguins have longer bills but lower body mass than Gentoo penguins.

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
section: Changing the Order of Penguin Species
text:
Changing the Order of Penguin Species
I use fct_relevel() to change the order of the species in the plot legend. I put Gentoo first, followed by Chinstrap and Adelie.

penguins_reordered <- penguins |>
  mutate(
    species = forcats::fct_relevel(
      species,
      "Gentoo",
      "Chinstrap",
      "Adelie"
    )
  )

penguins_reordered_plot <- ggplot(
  data = penguins_reordered,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  xlab("Bill length (mm)") +
  ylab("Body mass (g)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18))

penguins_reordered_plot

title: Exploring Penguin Measurements in R
text:
What I Learned
Changing the order of a factor changes how the species appear in the plot legend. It can also change which colour is assigned to each species. The penguin measurements and the positions of the points stay the same.
This exercise helped me understand how factor levels affect the presentation of a plot in R.

title: My First Week in the MDS Program
text:
Starting the Master of Data Science program at the University of British Columbia has marked an important transition in my academic and professional development. Building on the research, instructional design, and academic data analysis experience I developed during my PhD in Educational Psychology, I am now expanding my skills through graduate training in data science.
During the first week of the program, I have been developing practical experience with Python, R, Git, GitHub, Quarto, probability, and reproducible data analysis. I have also been learning how to use Git and GitHub to track changes to my work and how to build and publish a website using Quarto and GitHub Pages.



My first weeks in MDS.


My longer-term goal is to build strong expertise in machine learning and applied data science. I am particularly interested in combining my research background with computational and statistical methods to solve real-world problems. This portfolio will document my progress through the MDS program and provide examples of the technical and analytical skills I continue to develop.

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text: In this post, I use Python to explore beach measurements over time. I use pandas to calculate monthly averages and see how the measurements at each location compare with their overall average. I also use Altair to create a graph and look at how the measurements change over time.

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text: In this post, I use Python to explore beach measurements over time. I use pandas to calculate monthly averages and see how the measurements at each location compare with their overall average. I also use Altair to create a graph and look at how the measurements change over time.

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text:
Data Source
The data comes from the Narrabeen beach survey dataset, which contains beach width measurements from five locations at Narrabeen Beach in New South Wales, Australia, between 1980 and 2019. I used the beach_data.csv file provided in DSCI 511 Worksheet 7 for this analysis.
The original dataset is described in Turner, I. L., Harley, M. D., Short, A. D., et al. (2016). A multi-decade dataset of monthly beach profile surveys and inshore wave forcing at Narrabeen, Australia. Scientific Data, 3, 160024.

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text:
Reading the Data
I first read the CSV file into a pandas dataframe. I use the first column as the index and tell pandas to recognize the dates.

import pandas as pd

beach_df = pd.read_csv(

    index_col=0,

)

Comparing Measurements with the Average
I subtract each location’s overall monthly average from its monthly measurements. A negative value means the measurement was below that location’s average, while a positive value means it was above average.

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text:
Preparing the Data for Visualization
I reshape the data so that each row contains a date, a location, and its measurement difference. This will let me display all five locations in one graph.

beach_long = (
    beach_difference
    .reset_index()
    .melt(
        id_vars="index",
        var_name="location",
        value_name="difference"
    )
)

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text:
Visualizing Beach Width Changes
I use a heatmap to compare monthly beach measurements across the five locations. Each row represents one location, and each coloured cell represents one month. Blue indicates a measurement above that location’s overall average, while red indicates a measurement below its average.

import altair as alt

beach_chart = (
    alt.Chart(beach_long)
    .mark_rect()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("yearmonth(index):O", title="Month"),
        y=alt.Y("location:N", title="Beach location"),
        color=alt.Color(
            "difference:Q",
            title="Difference from average",
            scale=alt.Scale(scheme="redblue", domainMid=0)
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("index:T", title="Month", format="%B %Y"),
            alt.Tooltip("location:N", title="Location"),
            alt.Tooltip("difference:Q", title="Difference", format=".1f")
        ]
    )
    .properties(
        title="Monthly Beach Measurements Relative to Average",
        width=700,
        height=180
    )
)

beach_chart

title: Exploring Beach Width Changes Over Time
text:
What I Learned
The heatmap shows that beach measurements do not change in the same way at all five locations. Some months are above average at one location but below average at another. Comparing monthly differences from each location’s average shows how beach measurements change over time, while taking into account the different average measurements at the five locations.
